blocks.prompt: Why a Boat Floats
blocks.text: Put your hand into a full bath. The water climbs up the sides. Your hand pushed the water out of the way. A boat does the same thing, only bigger. The boat pushes water out of the way. The water pushes back up on the boat. That push is strong enough to hold the whole boat up. So the boat floats. Then the wind does the rest. It fills the sails and pushes the boat along.

blocks.prompt: Why a Steel Ship Floats and a Nail Does Not
blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. Drop a small steel nail into a bucket of water and it sinks straight to the bottom. Steel is much heavier than water. But a steel ship, as long as a street and loaded with cars, floats. How? The answer is not about weight. It is about shape. When anything sits in water, it shoves some water out of the way. The water shoves back. If the water it shoved aside weighs as much as the object does, the object floats. A solid nail is small, so it only shoves aside a tiny bit of water, and that tiny bit is far too light to hold the nail up. Down it goes. A ship is hollow. It is a huge steel bowl full of air. To sink low enough to swallow that ship, the sea has to be shoved aside by the ton. All that shoved water pushes back, and the ship stops sinking and rides there. Squash the same ship into a solid steel cube and it would drop like the nail. Shape is everything.

notes: A tight sail is a wing standing on its edge

blocks.prompt: The Impossible Direction
blocks.text: Sailing downwind is easy to picture. The wind comes from behind, fills the sails like a bag, and shoves the boat forward. Any raft with a bedsheet can do that. The clever part is that a sailboat can also sail toward the wind, and that seems impossible. Watch a boat leave a harbor into a headwind and it will get out anyway, leaning over, moving fast. Here is the trick. A sail is not really a bag. Pulled tight, it takes on a gentle curve, and that curve makes it a wing standing on its edge. Air arriving at an angle has to bend around the curve, and bending air has a price. The pressure on the outer face of the sail drops below the pressure on the inner face, and the sail is pulled hard toward the low pressure. That pull is not backward and it is not forward. It is roughly sideways, off to one side of the boat. Sideways is useless, so the boat cheats. Underneath the hull hangs a keel, a heavy fin slicing down into the water. Water is thick and stubborn. The keel refuses to move sideways through it. The sideways pull has nowhere to go, so it escapes in the only direction left, which is forward. The boat leans, and it goes. There is a limit. No ordinary sailboat can sail straight into the wind. Come within about 45 degrees of it and the sails flap uselessly. So sailors zigzag, cutting across the wind first one way and then the other, climbing toward it in steps. They call it tacking. It is slower than a straight line, and for thousands of years it was the difference between a coast you could leave and a coast you were stuck on.

blocks.prompt: Faster Than the Wind That Moves You
blocks.text: Common sense says a sailboat cannot outrun the wind pushing it. Once the boat matches the wind's speed, the wind should feel still, the sails should go slack, and that should be the end of it. Common sense is right, but only about one kind of sailing. Sail directly downwind and you are running a race you cannot win. The sail is doing nothing clever. It is a bag catching a shove, and the shove weakens as you speed up. A boat running dead downwind is always slower than the wind carrying it. Turn across the wind and the whole situation changes, because now the boat starts making weather of its own. Ride a bicycle on a still day and you feel a breeze in your face that did not exist before you started pedaling. You made it. A sailboat does the same. The wind a moving boat actually feels is the real wind combined with the wind of its own motion, and sailors call that combination the apparent wind. Here is the strange part. When a boat sails across the wind rather than away from it, going faster does not weaken the apparent wind. It strengthens it, and it swings it forward. More speed makes more wind. More wind makes more speed. Nothing is being created from nothing. The boat is not beating physics, it is trading. Its sail is a wing working in thin fast air. Its keel or its foils grip thick slow water. Caught between the two, the hull is squeezed forward like a wet melon seed pinched between two fingers. The energy still comes from the wind. The boat is simply an unusually good machine for taking it. The results are not small. An ice boat, with nothing but slick blades under it and almost no drag to fight, can travel three or four times the speed of the wind that drives it. Modern racing yachts lift their hulls clear of the water on carbon foils and do the same thing at sea, sailing near fifty knots in a twenty knot breeze. Those crews are not chasing the wind. They are outrunning it, using it, and making more of it as they go.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Oldest known boat: a hollowed pine log, about 10,000 years old
Boats are older than the wheel
On the Nile the current runs north, the wind blows south
A tight sail is a wing turned on its side
Hokulea sailed Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 with no instruments

blocks.prompt: The Machine That Turned the Sea Into a Road
blocks.text: For most of human history, water was a wall. It marked the place where a people ended. The boat is the machine that turned that wall into a road, and it did the job in stages, each one stranger than the last. The first stage was simply floating. The oldest boat anyone has found is a hollowed-out pine log dug from a peat bog at Pesse, in the Netherlands, and it is roughly ten thousand years old. That makes the boat older than the wheel. It is three meters of tree with the middle scraped out, and it works for the same reason a steel tanker works: a hollow object shoves aside more water than a solid one, and the shoved water pushes back. Weight was never the question. Shape was. The second stage was borrowing the wind, and the people who did it best early on lived along the Nile. That river is a gift with a rare piece of luck built into it. The current runs north toward the sea. The prevailing wind blows south, against the current. So an Egyptian boat could drift downstream to the delta on the current, raise a sail, and be pushed home again by the wind. The convenience ran so deep that it soaked into the writing itself. In hieroglyphs, the sign for traveling south is a boat with its sail up, and the sign for traveling north is a boat with the sail down. The language could not separate the direction from the machine. But a sail that only runs before the wind is a one-way ticket. You can leave; you cannot choose to come back. That is why the third stage matters more than the other two combined. Across many centuries and many coastlines, sailors worked out how to sail toward the wind. Pulled tight, a sail stops being a bag and becomes a wing turned on its side, and a wing does not get shoved. It gets pulled sideways, hard. A keel or a leeboard refuses to slide sideways through the water, so that sideways pull has only one place left to escape, and the boat squirts forward. It still cannot point straight into the wind, so sailors zigzag, climbing upwind in steps they call tacks. Slow, wet, and world-changing. The sea stopped being a current you obeyed and became a surface you could cross in any direction you chose. The Polynesians took this furthest, and earliest, with the least equipment. Sailing double-hulled canoes, they found and settled hundreds of islands scattered across millions of square miles of open Pacific, without a compass, a chart, or a clock. They navigated by memorized star paths, by the direction of swells felt through the hull at night, by the flight lines of birds at dusk, by the color of clouds standing over land they could not yet see. For a long time European scholars insisted this was luck, that such voyages must have been accidental drifts. In 1976 a double-hulled canoe named Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti carrying no instruments at all, navigated the old way by a man named Mau Piailug, and settled the argument at sea rather than on paper. We treat all of this as finished and ordinary now. It is not. Roughly eighty percent of the world's traded goods still cross the ocean in a hull, and the whole arrangement rests on one stubborn idea somebody had a very long time ago: that the water in your way and the wind against you are not obstacles. They are the engine, if you are shaped correctly.
